sections.title: Is the SpO₂ Real?
items: Some 'refractory hypoxemia' is measurement error — verify before escalating.
**Poor pleth:** = cold/vasoconstricted, shock, tremor, gripping bedrail, nail polish/artificial nails, probe detached or over a BP-cuff arm, venous pulsations
Cross-check another finger, an ear/forehead probe, or ABG if uncertain
Comfortable & talking at SpO₂ 73% → confirm the number before intubating; looks terrible at SpO₂ 94% → !!believe the patient, not the monitor!!
**Methemoglobinemia**: SpO₂ ~85% with normal/high PaO₂ → co-oximetry; think dapsone, benzocaine, nitrates/nitrites, topical anesthetics
**Carbon monoxide**: pulse-ox falsely reassuring → get carboxyhemoglobin/co-oximetry if exposure plausible
Targets: SpO₂ 94–98% (88–92% if CO₂-retention risk); !!don't leave stable patients at 100%!!

pairs.value: Hypoxemia is a finding — treatment depends on the mechanism. Don't reflexively escalate NC→NRB→HFNC→BiPAP→intubation without asking WHY. Type 1: ↓ PaO2 with nl/↓ PaCO2 (initially); ↑A-a gradient

Cardiogenic (CHF, flash pulm edema, valvular) or noncardiogenic (ARDS, neurogenic); ↑FiO₂ helps V/Q mismatch; shunt physiology (ARDS, dense PNA, lobar collapse) poorly responsive to O₂ — needs PEEP/recruitment
CAP, HAP, VAP, aspiration; viral (COVID, influenza); opportunistic if immunocompromised; dense consolidation → shunt physiology

pairs.key: PE — V/Q mismatch / low mixed-venous O₂
pairs.value: Clear lungs + hypoxia + tachycardia + risk factors; massive PE = ↓ BP + ↓ CO amplifying hypoxemia; fix = restore CO/RV afterload — !!NOT more PEEP!!
Spontaneous, traumatic, iatrogenic; tension PTX = ↓ BP + tracheal deviation: needle decompression
B/l infiltrates, PaO2/FiO2 <300, not fully explained by cardiac failure; shunt → ↑FiO₂ gives little improvement; needs recruitment/PEEP, prone; triggers: sepsis, aspiration, PNA, pancreatitis, TRALI
Opioid/sedation, NM disease, OHS, COPD, CNS disease; nl A-a gradient; check PaCO₂/pH — needs ventilation, not just O₂ (see Acute Hypercapnic RF)
↓ cardiac output (RV failure, cardiogenic shock, severe PH) amplifies any hypoxemia. Fix = ↑CO / ↓RV afterload / ↑perfusion — !!NOT more PEEP!!
ILD, pulmonary vascular disease — rarely the sole cause of abrupt severe inpatient hypoxemia

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** ABG/VBG, CBC, BMP, lactate, troponin, BNP
-**Orders:** CXR (portable), continuous SpO2, POCUS (B-lines, lung sliding), IV access x2, telemetry
Sit the pt up, give supplemental O2, confirm good O2 pleth, & escalate to HFNC or NIPPV based on WOB & oxygenation.
**HFNC** for hypoxemic failure: ~1 cmH2O PEEP per 10 L/min; better tolerated than NIPPV
**BiPAP/NIPPV** for cardiogenic pulmonary edema if pt is awake & protecting airway (↓ WOB, recruits alveoli)
--Bipap Settings: ****
**Intubate** if refractory hypoxemia, cant protect airway, severe fatigue, or hemodynamic instability.
--Clarify code status / GOC before intubation
--Call anesthesia/ICU
--Order sedation per anesthesia
**Postintubation ↓ BP** : c/f **tension PTX** (b/l breath sounds?), autoPEEP (disconnect vent briefly), ↓ preload from PEEP, vs sedation-induced vasodilation
-Lung protective ventilation in ARDS: TV 6 mL/kg IBW, Pplat<30 cmH2O, PEEP per ARDSNet table, permissive hypercapnia
**Treat cause:** nitrates/diuresis/NIPPV for SCAPE/pulmonary edema, abx for PNA, AC for PE, & decompression for tension PTX.
POCUS is faster than CXR: B-lines (edema), lung sliding (PTX), IVC (volume), EF (cardiac function); can guide management in realtime
--ABG: confirm hypoxemia (PaO2, A-a gradient); calculate P/F ratio to grade ARDS
--CXR: Infiltrates (pneumonia, edema, ARDS), PTX, effusion, cardiomegaly
--EKG: RV strain (PE), ischemia (ACS: flash pulm edema), dysrhythmia
--CBC: ↑ WBC (infection), anemia (↓ O2 carrying capacity)
--BMP: Lytes, renal function, anion gap (metabolic acidosis)
--Troponin: if ACS or massive PE suspected
--Lactate: tissue hypoperfusion, shock
--CTA chest: if PE suspected & pt can tolerate (ignore Cr in an emergency)

pairs.key: NIV weaker in de novo hypoxemia
pairs.value: Pneumonia/ARDS — large spontaneous Vt & high transpulmonary pressure → P-SILI and delayed intubation. HFNC preferred.

sections.title: When to Intubate & Preoxygenation
items: Trajectory beats a magic number — intubate the patient who will fail in the next hour, not the peri-arrest one.
Intubate: arrest from hypoxemia, SpO₂ <88% or P/F <60 despite maximal support (2024 AHRF consensus)
Strongly consider: shock needing pressor, worsening distress/AMS/hypoxemia, SpO₂ <92% or P/F <100 despite max support, pH <7.30
Preoxygenate with NIV (PREOXI 2024: peri-intubation hypoxemia 9% vs 18% with mask): FiO₂ 100%, EPAP ≥5, IPAP ≥10, RR ≥10, ~3 min; HFNC underneath for apneic oxygenation
Peri-intubation BP is as important as SpO₂ — if MAP marginal, start norepinephrine 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min BEFORE induction, not after arrest
Ready before induction: pressor connected, **working IV**, suction, video laryngoscope, BVM + PEEP valve, RT, experienced operator

sections.title: Pulmonary HTN / RV Failure — Intubation Can Kill

pairs.value: RV hates hypoxemia, hypercapnia, acidosis, high mean airway pressure, hypotension, ↓venous return. Sedation→vasodilation→↓RV coronary perfusion, PPV→↓preload, ↑PVR → RV output falls → PEA. Avoid intubation when possible (ESC/ERS).
Correct hypoxemia/hypercapnia/acidosis; POCUS the RV; find the trigger (PE, infection, arrhythmia, volume overload, LV failure, stopped PAH therapy).
!!Do NOT abruptly interrupt IV epoprostenol or IV/SC treprostinil!! — rebound PH can be fatal. A disconnected prostacyclin line is an emergency.
Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg or carefully dosed ketamine (avoid large propofol); norepinephrine ± vasopressin running, keep MAP >60; avoid high PEEP/hypercapnia but not zero PEEP.

Inhaled epoprostenol ~50 ng/kg/min (wean ~10 ng/kg/min) or iNO ~20 ppm — ↓PVR, unload RV, improve V/Q & oxygenation. Bridge/rescue only (no mortality benefit in routine ARDS); use WITH proning/lung-protective vent. Consider peri-intubation in severe RV failure or R→L shunt.

sections.title: ARDS — Prone Early & Rescue
items: Lung-protective: Vt 6 mL/kg predicted body weight (not actual), Pplat <30; drop toward 4–5 mL/kg if Pplat high; PEEP to maintain recruitment
Prone EARLY if P/F <150 after optimization — ≥16 h/session (ESICM 2023, strong rec; PROSEVA). Don't save it for peri-arrest.
Proning also improves V/Q, reduces regional lung stress, drains secretions, can unload the RV (matters in cor pulmonale)

Rescue sequence: exclude mechanical problem (ETT position, mainstem, plug, pneumothorax, circuit) → optimize PEEP → prone → adequate sedation → correct dyssynchrony → NMB if needed → inhaled vasodilator → recheck RV → call ECMO center early
Be cautious with aggressive recruitment maneuvers — high pressures overdistend normal lung, ↓venous return, worsen RV afterload, cause barotrauma

sections.title: Refractory Hypoxemia — Find the Cause
items: Before calling it 'refractory': is the pulse-ox real? Is O₂ actually flowing, FiO₂ set correctly, device fitting (mouth-breather on a nasal device, NRB bag inflated, HFNC connected)?
Mechanical/lung: pneumothorax, mainstem ETT, mucus plug, ETT/circuit obstruction, auto-PEEP, severe bronchospasm, new PE, edema, atelectasis, aspiration, new intracardiac R→L shunt
Physiology: collapsing cardiac output, severe RV failure, profound anemia, methemoglobinemia, stopped prostacyclin, excessive PEEP worsening RV output, exhausted respiratory muscles
Intubated + sudden desat → run DOPES and check peak vs plateau (see Ventilator Troubleshooting & Sedation)

Single-lung-disease trap: with unilateral pneumonia/plug/collapse, ↑PEEP can overdistend the good lung and divert blood to the bad lung → worse V/Q. If ↑PEEP worsens oxygenation, stop assuming 'more PEEP.'
'Good lung down' can improve oxygenation in unilateral disease (exception: massive hemoptysis → bleeding lung down to protect the other)

Mucus plug / lobar collapse: sudden O₂ need in weak-cough, postop, neuro, or trach patients — suction, reposition, chest PT, mobilize, humidify, bronchoscopy if persistent. A plug causes major hypoxemia before radiographic collapse appears.

pairs.value: Sudden hypoxemia within ~6 h of transfusion — distinguish the two; don't reflexively furosemide every post-transfusion desat.
Volume overload: HTN, JVD, pulmonary edema, positive fluid balance. Tx: O₂/NIV, loop diuretic, afterload reduction.
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema ± hypotension, no volume overload. Tx: stop transfusion, notify blood bank, supportive / ARDS-style ventilation.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Letting patient sit on 6 L NC for hours because SpO₂ is 'still 91%'
Treating the SpO₂% instead of the work of breathing
BiPAP indefinitely for pneumonia despite obvious NIV failure; assuming every hypoxemic patient needs BiPAP
Waiting for a CXR before treating obvious tension pneumothorax
Intubating severe PAH without preparing for cardiovascular collapse; cranking PEEP into a failing RV
Waiting too long to prone severe ARDS; using inhaled epoprostenol instead of (not in addition to) proning
Forgetting mucus plugging postop/in weak patients; assuming a normal CXR excludes major atelectasis
Intubating massive-PE hypoxemia while ignoring the obstructed pulmonary circulation
Abruptly interrupting chronic epoprostenol/treprostinil

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** ABG/VBG, BMP (bicarb), CBC
-**Orders:** CXR (portable), continuous SpO2, waveform capnography, IV access, telemetry
Use BiPAP early for hypercapnic failure; titrate IPAP for ventilation (CO2), EPAP for oxygenation. Also for CHF + pulmonary edema if awake & protecting airway.
- Do NOT withhold O2 in COPD: !!hypoxia kills faster than CO2 retention!!; target SpO2 88–92% in known CO2 retainers, but treat hypoxia first
Treat cause: bronchodilators + steroids for COPD/asthma; Mg for refractory severe asthma; naloxone for opioid OD
Silent chest in asthma = BAD: no air movement; if PaCO2 is nl. or rising in acute asthma = impending respiratory arrest
Intubate if worsening hypercapnia/acidemia (pH <7.25 with rising PaCO2 despite BiPAP), cant protect airway, severe fatigue, or hemodynamic instability.
-For asthma/COPD intubation: low RR (8-12), long expiratory time (I:E 1:4-5), watch for autoPEEP (breath stacking); disconnect vent if hemodynamic collapse
Neuromuscular weakness (MG, GBS): trend NIF & FVC, intubate electively before crash; clear lungs + hypoxia may be NM weakness
Postintubation ↓ BP : c/f tension PTX (b/l breath sounds?), autoPEEP (disconnect vent briefly), ↓preload from positive pressure, sedationinduced vasodilation
POCUS is faster than CXR: Blines (edema), lung sliding (PTX), IVC (volume), EF (cardiac function); can guide management in realtime
Clarify code status / GOC before intubation: this conversation is essential

BNP/NTproBNP: differentiates cardiogenic (CHF) from pulmonary cause (BNP >500 pg/mL suggests CHF)

rapid afterload reduction: Start nitroglycerin ASAP. If taking too long to give to pt, bridge with SL nitroglycerin.
Dont reflexively give diuretics. Recheck volume after NIPPV and nitrates control the hypertension; add loop diuretic later if true overload is present.

sections.title: Characteristic X-Ray
items: Typical film shows bilateral pulmonary vascular congestion with interstitial or alveolar edema in a central bat-wing distribution.

drugs.name: Nitroglycerin
drugs.dose: 0.4 mg SL q5 min while setting up IV; IV infusion 100 mcg/min and titrate rapidly upward as needed
drugs.contraindications: SBP <100, PDE5 inhibitor use, severe aortic stenosis
drugs.notes: First-line therapy in SCAPE. High doses provide arterial vasodilation and afterload reduction; use BP and WOB to guide titration.

drugs.name: Furosemide
drugs.dose: 40-80 mg IV, or ~2-2.5x home oral dose
drugs.contraindications: Hypovolemia, severe hypokalemia
drugs.notes: Use after BP and respiratory distress are controlled if true volume overload is present. It is slower and less helpful than early NIPPV plus nitrates in SCAPE.

drugs.name: Nitroprusside
drugs.dose: 0.5 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate to BP; avoid prolonged high-dose use
drugs.contraindications: Hypotension; caution with renal failure and prolonged infusion
drugs.notes: Alternative vasodilator when severe afterload excess persists despite nitroglycerin.

pairs.value: Sympathetic crashing acute pulmonary edema (SCAPE).
acute ↑ afterload --> pulmonary edema and ↓ forward flow-->sympathetic surge -->↑↑ afterload.
Unlike slower CHF exacerbation or hypotensive cardiogenic shock, SCAPE is usually very hypertensive and can worsen over minutes.
Rapid NIPPV and afterload reduction matter most; diuretics less important.

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Sudden pleuritic chest pain + dyspnea + tachycardia + hypoxia with clear lungs; risk factors: immobility, malignancy, surgery, or prior VTE; massive PE = hemodynamic collapse from acute RV pressure overload
Hemodynamics: SBP <90 or MAP <60 = Category DE: activate PERT
Tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxia: apply R modifier if supplemental O2 needed
JVD, loud P2, RV heave: signs of RV strain/pressure overload
Unilateral leg swelling, calf tenderness, Homan sign (unreliable): concurrent DVT
Mentation: AMS, obtundation (endorgan hypoperfusion: Category D2 or E)
Skin: cool, mottled arms/legs (cardiogenic shock)
Auscultation: clear lungs (PEhas clear lungs), new TR murmur

pairs.value: Major surgery, trauma, immobilization, cancer, pregnancy/OCP: tx duration 3-6 months
No identifiable risk factor: consider extended anticoagulation (>3-6 mo), ageappropriate cancer screening
Chest pain, ↑ troponin, ST changes: EKG & echo help differentiate. PE causes RV ischemia with troponin rise
Tearing chest/back pain, BP differential, wide mediastinum. Thrombolysis is lethal if dissection
Sudden dyspnea, unilateral absent breath sounds, ↓ BP if tension

Wheezing, prolonged expiration, hx of obstructive disease: but PE can coexist

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** D-dimer, troponin, BNP, BMP, CBC, coags
-**Orders:** CT-PA (if stable), bilateral LE dopplers, EKG (S1Q3T3, sinus tach, RBBB), CXR, IV access x2, continuous SpO2, telemetry
Confirm diagnosis
Use CTPA; use V/Q scan if contrast is contraindicated
check clot burden and RV size on CT
check hemodynamic stability
Hemodynamically unstable > Category E
Transient or recurrent hypotension responsive to fluids > Category D
Normotensive > proceed to risk stratification
Risk stratify with sPESI, PESI, or Hestia
Lowrisk > Category B
Elevated risk > Category C
For Category C: check RV function and biomarkers
RV dysfunction plus elevated troponin > Category C3
RV dysfunction or elevated troponin alone > Category C2
Neither > Category C1
Add R modifier if hypoxemic or requiring supplemental O2
Start anticoagulation immediately
Category AC: DOAC preferred, or LMWH then DOAC
Category DE: UFH or LMWH; UFH preferred if advanced therapy may be needed
For most pts, LMWH is preferred over UFH
Category C3: watch 72h: PEITHO shock occurs @ ~1.5-1.8 days. Serial vitals, trop, lactate q6-12h
Cat DE post thrombolysis: restart heparin when aPTT <80. Watch for bleeding (esp ICH). Repeat TTE at 24-48h to check RV recovery
Transition to DOAC when stable: apixaban 10mg BID x7d> 5mg BID or rivaroxaban 15mg BID x21d> 20mg daily
Duration of AC: provoked with major reversible RF: 3-6 mo. Unprovoked: consider indefinite. Cancer: indefinite (DOAC or LMWH)
IVC filter: If Abs CI to AC, & acute proximal DVT. Remove when anticoagulation can started/4 weeks. NOT suggested routinely
Followup within 1 week of discharge (Class I): check adherence, bleeding, sx
3 month visit: recheck anticoagulation duration, screen for persistent sx/dyspnea (CTEPD risk)
**CTA Chest (CTPE):** Best PE dx. RV/LV ratio >0.9 on CT = RV dysfunction (helps categorize C vs D)
**Ddimer:** For lowith intermediate pretest probability only (PERC negative + Wells ≤4). Ageadjusted: < age × 10 ng/mL IF >50
**Troponin:** ↑ troponin = myocardial injury from RV strain. differentiates C1 vs C2/C3
**BNP/NTproBNP:** ↑ = RV strain. Comb with trop & RV imaging for risk strat
**Lactate:** ↑ lactate >2 mmol/L = tissue hypoperfusion (Cat D2)
**TTE (echocardiogram):** C/D. check RV/LV ratio, RV diameter, TAPSE, RVSP, McConnell sign, septal bowing, IVC collapse
**EKG:** Sinus tach (most common), S1Q3T3, RBBB, RV strain (TWI V1V4), right axis
**ABG/VBG:** Hypoxemia, resp. alkalosis, ↑ A gradient. nl. ABG does not r/o PE
**LE duplex US:** If CTPA unavailable or contraindicated. DVT found in ~50% of PE pts

**Wells Score / sPESI:** [Wells PE](https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/115/wellscriteriapulmonaryembolism) for pretest probability. [sPESI](https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/1247/simplified-pesi-pulmonary-embolism-severity-index) for severity: 0 = low risk (Cat B); ≥1 = elevated (Cat C+)

drugs.name: Enoxaparin/Lovenox (LMWH)
drugs.dose: 1 mg/kg SC q12h or 1.5 mg/kg SC daily
drugs.contraindications: CrCl <30 (use UFH), active bleed, plt <50k
drugs.notes: Preferred over UFH for initial parenteral tx (Class I, 2026 AHA/ACC). Predictable pharmacokinetics, no monitoring.

drugs.name: Heparin (UFH)
drugs.contraindications: Active bleed, HIT
drugs.notes: Use for Category DE (may need thrombolysis: UFH is titratable & shortacting), CrCl <30, obesity, or when rapid reversal may needed. Goal aPTT 60-80 sec.

drugs.name: Norepinephrine +/ Vasopressin
drugs.dose: Norepinephrine 0.05-0.5 mcg/kg/min IV; add vasopressin 0.04 U/min
drugs.contraindications: No absolute CI in shock; use caution with severe ischemia or extravasation risk
drugs.notes: Preferred vasopressor approach for hypotensive PE with RV failure. Norepinephrine supports MAP with less tachycardia than epinephrine; add vasopressin (decreases PVR) when escalating pressor support or when catecholamine burden is high.

drugs.name: Epinephrine
drugs.contraindications: Relative: marked tachyarrhythmia or severe myocardial ischemia
drugs.notes: Reasonable if profound shock or periarrest & you need both inotropy & vasopressor effect quickly, but higher arrhythmia & lactate burden than levo +/ vaso.

drugs.name: Alteplase (tPA): full dose
drugs.contraindications: Active hemorrhage, CVA <3 mo, intracranial neoplasm, recent surgery <3 wk, aortic dissection
drugs.notes: Hold heparin during infusion, restart when aPTT <80. ~10% risk of severe bleeding, 1.7% risk of ICH.

drugs.name: Alteplase: ↓ dose
drugs.contraindications: Same as full dose
drugs.notes: Trending toward similar efficacy with less bleeding. Option in pts with relative CI.

drugs.name: Alteplase: catheter directed (CDL)
drugs.contraindications: Same as systemic, plus vascular access contraindications
drugs.notes: For Cat DE when considering lysis. May reduce major bleeding vs systemic.<5mg per PA NOT suggested over 5-10mg (Class 3, no benefit). Not suggested for Cat AC1.

drugs.name: Apixaban
drugs.dose: 10mg PO BID x 7 days, then 5mg PO BID
drugs.contraindications: Severe hepatic dz, triplepositive APS
drugs.notes: DOAC alternative. Lowest bleeding risk in trials. Can use with CrCl 1530 (advantage over rivaroxaban). No bridging needed.

drugs.name: Rivaroxaban
drugs.dose: 15mg PO BID x 21 days, then 20mg PO daily
drugs.contraindications: CrCl <30, severe hepatic dz, triplepositive APS
drugs.notes: DOACs preferred over warfarin (Class I, 2026 AHA/ACC). No bridging needed: start directly. Take with food for absorption.

drugs.name: Tenecteplase
drugs.contraindications: Same as alteplase
drugs.notes: Single IV bolus: easier administration than alteplase infusion. Studied in PEITHO trial (halfdose). Not FDAapproved for PE but used offlabel.

pairs.value: Replaces massive/submassive/low-risk with Categories A–E based on clinical severity, biomarkers, RV imaging, hemodynamics, & respiratory status
Cardiopulmonary failure: systemic thrombolysis is first line; consider ↓dose alteplase in selected pts & activate PERT now
Incipient failure: consider thrombolysis if bleeding risk is acceptable; catheter directed therapy may reduce bleeding risk; activate PERT
C3 needs monitored admission, anticoagulation, & close reassessment for 72h; C1C2 need admission, anticoagulation, & serial assessment
Lowrisk ptsget anticoagulation alone; LMWH is preferred initially, & DOACs are preferred over warfarin when appropriate
Subclinical: aS/S PE, incidental finding. ok to DC
Symptomatic, low clinical severity (PESI≤85,sPESI=0, Bova≤4). B1 = subseg, B2 =nonsubseg. Early DC
Symptomatic, elevated clinical severity (PESI >85, sPESI ≥1, Bova >4). C1 = nl RV + nl biomarkers. C2 = abn RV OR ↑ biomarkers. C3 = abn RV & ↑ biomarkers (highest intermediate risk)
Incipient cardiopulm failure. D1 = transient ↓ BP (SBP <90 for <15min or fluid resp). D2 = normotensive shock (lactate >2, AKI, UOP <0.5 mL/kg/h, AMS, CI <2.2, MAP <60)
Cardiopulm failure: persistent ↓ BP /shock. E1 = HD collapse with cardiogenic shock (SCAI C). E2 = refractory cardiogenic shock (SCAI DE) or cardiac arrest
Added when hypoxemia, ↑HR, or needs O2/ventilation (e.g., C3R, D2R)

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Sudden respiratory distress or obstruction in a patient with a tracheostomy — first check if the tube is patent, then displaced, then consider false passage; remove the tube and bag via stoma if in doubt
Air mvmt through trach: place hand over trach opening to feel airflow
Stomal site: eryma, purulence, crepitus, granulation tissue, bleeding
Auscultate lungs b/l: ↓ breath sounds: Obst., dislodgement, or pneumothorax
Subcutaneous emphysema around stoma (false passage or pneumomediastinum)

pairs.value: Mucus plugging (most common), blood clot, granulation tissue, false passage, tube malposition. Bronchoscopy may needed for granulation tissue or malposition dx
Accidental decannulation, pt selfremoval, loose trach ties, coughing, obesity (deep stoma tract)
Granulation tissue at stoma, suctioning trauma, peristomal skin breakdown. Usually selflimited.

Tracheoinnominate fistula (TIF): hemorrhage from erosion into brachiocephalic artery. ~3 days–6 weeks post trach. ~100% Mortality w/o intervention, 64.5% overall. Mild bleed> massive hemorrhage in 44% of cases (typically within 1 week)
Stomal cellulitis, tracheitis, abscess, VAP/tracheostomyassociated pneumonia

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** ABG/VBG
-**Orders:** Bedside suction, BVM at bedside, emergency trach kit at bedside, ENT consult, CXR, continuous SpO2
If still Obst after inner cannula removal: deflate cuff & remove entire trach tube
Try to reinsert trach tube (use one size smaller if difficulty). Use obturator for insertion.
Tube obstruction/dislodgement: Remove inner cannula, suction aggressively, provide oxygen at face & stoma, & replace tracheostomy if trained personnel & equipment are available.
Call airway/ENT/anesthesia early. If trach replacement fails, attempt oral intubation if anatomy permits; if not, ventilate through stoma.
Bleeding: Sentinel bleeding can precede tracheoinnominate fistula. Overinflate cuff, try to manually compress, & move now toward operative control.
Infection / local issues: Treat stomal cellulitis, tracheitis, mucus plugging, cuff problems, or false passage based on cause while maintaining airway patency throughout.
Bedside equipment: Always have at bedside: trach tube one size smaller, obturator, ETTs (6.0–7.0), BVM, suction with catheters, spare inner cannula, 10 mL syringe for cuff
Predischarge: All pts & caregivers receive emergency trach management education & maintain emergency supplies (spare trach, suction, BVM) at all times
**Stat:** SpO2, VBG/ABG, CBC, BMP, type & screen (if bleeding)
**Imaging:** CXR: tube position, pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysema
**If bleeding:** Type & crossmatch, coags (PT/INR, PTT), fibrinogen. CT angiography if TIF suspected (if stable enough)
**If infection:** Sputum culture, BCxs, wound culture if purulent stomal drainage

sections.title: TracheoInnominate Fistula (TIF) Protocol
items: initial bleed: scant BRB: massive hemorrhage —> treat as TIF until proven otherwise
Activate MTP: anticipate massive hemorrhage
Call ENT/surgery STAT: tx is emergent OR
Hyperinflate cuff: inflate with 50 cc air to tamponade bleeding vessel against sternum (controls hemorrhage success ~70%)
If fails: remove trach, intubate orally (advance ETT distal to fistula site) & inflate ETT cuff past bleeding point
Digital innominate artery compression: insert finger through stoma, compress artery anteriorly against posterior sternum
Maintain digital pressure during transport to OR
Sentinel bleeding (minor hemoptysis) precedes massive hemorrhage in 44% of TIF cases,within 1 week: warrants urgent bronchoscopy & imaging
Txt: open surgical ligation of innominate artery or endovascular occlusion (comparable success rates)
Mortality ~64.5% overall, ~100% without intervention: rapid recognition & temporization are critical

items: **Classic presentation**: Severe bronchospasm with accessory muscle use, inability to speak in full sentences, and significant work of breathing; silent chest = no air movement = impending respiratory arrest — treat aggressively
Concerning findings:
Severe WOB, unable to speak full sentences
Silent chest or markedly ↓ air movement: ominous, suggests critical Obst.
AMS, exhaustion, accessory muscle fatigue
Cyanosis
Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg (>15-20 mmHg =severe)
Rising EtCO2: esp if previously low, normalizing in tiring pt (fatigue, NOT improvement)
check: air entry bilaterally, wheezing (diffuse vs focal), RR, HR, accessory muscle use, diaphoresis, ability to speak, tripod positioning

Falling pH on ABG/VBG
AMS: confusion, somnolence, agitation
Silent chest: no wheezing = no air movement
Pulsus paradoxus >15-20 mmHg
SpO2 <90% despite NRB or high flow O2
Accessory muscle fatigue: pt is tiring out
PEF <100 L/min or <25% predicted
Normalizing CO2 + pt in distress = fatigue, NOT improvement> intubation

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** ABG/VBG (if severe or altered), BMP (K+ — albuterol lowers), CBC
-**Orders:** Peak flow (if able), continuous SpO2, CXR (r/o PTX), IV access, telemetry

Stabilize O2 & airflow now: give O2 to keep SpO2 >92%, albuterol Intermittent: 5mg q20min x3, then 2.5-10mg q1-4hr as needed OR Continuous 10-15mg/hr, Levalbuterol if significant tachycardia [5] Ipratropium 0.25-0.5mg q20min & recheck air movement/ WOB after every treatment cycle
methylprednisolone 60-125 mg IV = prednisone 40-60 mg PO early (IV/PO equally effective).
If still severe> add MGSO4 2g IV over ~20 min

Escalate before the crash: if pt tiring, CO2 is rising, or air movement getting worse> call ICU / airway help, NIPPV if possible: max insp support (insp pressure 8, Peep 0-3), & consider IM epinephrine or SC terbutaline for refractory severe bronchospasm while setting up the next step

Move to airway control & postintubation stabilization if failing: intubate for exhaustion, worsening AMS, silent chest, severe acidosis, refractory hypoxemia, or periarrest. After intubation, use low RR, long expiratory time, permissive hypercapnia, & watch closely for autoPEEP, hypotension, & pneumothorax
**ABG or VBG:** worsening status, or impending resp failure. Normalizing CO2 in distressed pt = danger sign
**BMP + Mg:** Lytes, renal function. ↓ K from albuterol. Make sure Mg repleted
**CBC:** Eosinophilia (allergic), ↑ WBC (infection vs steroid effect)
**PEF:** If pt can do it without delaying tx. <100 L/min or <40% predicted = severe. <25% predicted =high risk
**CXR:** Only if C/F pneumothorax, PNA, aspiration, edema, or alternative dx. Not routine
**Lactate:** May be ↑ from WOB, ↑ catecholamines, or albuterol (betaagonist effect: not always tissue hypoperfusion)
**EtCO2:** If available. Rising EtCO2 = worsening Obst. or fatigue

sections.title: Intubation & Vent Strategy
items: Indications for intubation: AMS, progressive fatigue, rising PaCO2/EtCO2 + distress, resp acidosis, silent chest, persistent hypoxemia, arrest/periarrest, NIPPV failure
RSI: ketamine (bronchodilatory) ispreferred induction agent. Avoid histaminereleasing agents
AC mode
RR 8-10/min; start slow; avoid air trapping
If Pplat >30 > lower RR
Low I:E >prolonged expiratory time
Low peak pressure> avoid breath stacking > correcting CO2
VT 6-8 mL/kg IBW
PEEP 0-5
Flow 80-100 L/min
FiO2 100%; titrate down fast
If Pplat still >30 > think PTX, misplaced ETT, edema
Permissive hypoventilation / hypercapnia OK; goal pH >7.2, Pplat <30
Deep sedation required. NMB if severe dyssynchrony or marked autoPEEP
If postintubation ↓ BP: c/f autoPEEP: take off vent briefly to allow exhalation (can be lifesaving). Also r/o PTX

drugs.name: Albuterol ( neb)
drugs.contraindications: Severe tachyarrhythmia (relative)
drugs.notes: Firstline. Some centers use higher doses in extreme cases. Monitor HR, K

drugs.name: Ipratropium
drugs.dose: 0.5mg neb q20min x3 doses, then q4-6h
drugs.contraindications: Acute angleclosure glaucoma (neb to eyes)
drugs.notes: Add to albuterol for severe exacerbations. Anticholinergic bronchodilator

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone
drugs.dose: 60-125mg IV initial dose, then scheduled dosing
drugs.contraindications: Active untreated infection (relative)
drugs.notes: Give early: takes 4-6h for full effect. Transition to PO prednisone 40-60mg when able

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.contraindications: Renal failure (use cautiously), myasnia gravis
drugs.notes: Smooth muscle relaxation. Single dose. Monitor for ↓ BP, flushing

drugs.name: Epinephrine (IM)
drugs.contraindications: Use cautiously in elderly, CAD, severe HTN
drugs.notes: For anaphylaxis, angioedema, or refractory severe bronchospasm. IV infusion in ICU for refractory cases

drugs.name: Terbutaline
drugs.contraindications: Tachyarrhythmia, severe CAD
drugs.notes: Beta2 agonist. Can consider infusion in refractory cases

drugs.name: Ketamine
drugs.dose: 0.5-2 mg/kg IV bolus; can follow with infusion
drugs.contraindications: Relative: uncontrolled HTN, ↑ ICP
drugs.notes: Bronchodilatory properties. Useful for severe agitation, periintubation sedation, or dissociative dose for RSI

drugs.name: Heliox (80:20 or 70:30)
drugs.dose: inhalation via tightfitting mask or vent
drugs.contraindications: High FiO2 requirement (heliox requires low FiO2 blend to be effective)
drugs.notes: ↓ Airflow resistance via lower gas density. Most useful if FiO2 requirement is low. Not universally available

Or <40% predicted: suggests severe exacerbation
Very high risk: consider early intubation
Air trapping from incomplete exhalation: ↑ intrathoracic pressure: ↓ venous return: ↓ BP. Key concern during mechanical ventilation
Intrinsic PEEP from air trapping. Worse by high RR, short expiratory time, or breath stacking
Accepting ↑ PaCO2 if pH ≥~7.15 & hemodynamics acceptable: avoids dangerous vent settings/barotrauma
Normalizing/rising CO2 in distressed pt = impending failure. Postintubation ↓ BP: think autoPEEP, disconnect vent briefly. Avoid breath stacking. Watch for ↓ K from albuterol

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Stridor + voice changes + work of breathing from obstruction above the carina; inspiratory stridor = supraglottic/glottic, expiratory = subglottic/tracheal, biphasic = critical; causes include infection, allergy, angioedema, or foreign body
Stridor: inspiratory = supraglottic/glottic. Expiratory = subglottic/tracheal. Biphasic = fixed glottic/subglottic lesion
Voice changes: hotpotato voice (supraglottic: epiglottitis, peritonsillar abscess), hoarseness (glottic: vocal cord pathology)
Air movement: present (partial) vs absent (complete: emergency)
Drooling, inability to swallow secretions: suggests supraglottic edema or mass
Tripod positioning, neck extension: pt optimizing airway
Neck exam: swelling, tenderness, crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema), tracheal deviation, expanding hematoma
Floor of mouth: woody/brawny induration, tongue protrusion ( Ludwig angina)
Oropharynx: peritonsillar bulging (PTA), uvular deviation: avoid in suspected epiglottitis in children
Trismus: suggests deep space infection (Ludwig, parapharyngeal, masticator space)
Cyanosis, ↓ SpO2, accessory muscle use, paradoxical chest/Abd movement

pairs.value: Sudden onset choking, coughing, stridor. Food bolus most common in adults (esp elderly, intoxicated, dentures, neurologic dysphagia)
Rapidonset laryngeal/tongue/lip swelling. Histaminemed. (epi responsive) vs bradykininmed. (ACEI: does NOT respond to epi/steroids/antihistamines, needs icatibant or C1INH)
Severe sore throat out of proportion to exam, dysphagia, drooling, muffled/hotpotato voice, stridor, fever. Lateral neck XR: thumbprint sign. Do NOT agitate
Bilateral submandibular/sublingual/submental space infection. Woody floor of mouth, tongue protrusion, trismus. 85% odontogenic origin. Airway emergency
Unilateral tonsillar bulging, uvular deviation, trismus, hotpotato voice. Needle aspiration or I&D
Neck stiffness, dysphagia, drooling, fever. CT neck with contrast. ↑ risk of mediastinitis if ruptures
Laryngeal edema from intubation. Risk factors: prolonged intubation, large ETT, traumatic intubation, female. Cuffleak test can predict
Postsurgical (thyroid, carotid, spine), anticoagulated. Expanding hematoma = open neck at bedside if airway compromised
Sudden glottic closure from irritation (secretions, blood, extubation). Positive pressure, jaw thrust, small dose succinylcholine (0.1-0.3 mg/kg IV) or topical lidocaine
Progressive stridor, hoarseness, dysphagia. Laryngeal, thyroid, mediastinal masses. May need awake fiberoptic intubation or tracheostomy
Burns to face/oropharynx, singed nasal hairs, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness. Intubate early: edema worsens over 12-24h
Bilateral = stridor & obstruction. Postthyroidectomy (recurrent laryngeal nerve injury), intubation trauma, neurologic causes

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** CBC, BMP
-**Orders:** Continuous SpO2, bedside laryngoscope + video laryngoscope + surgical airway kit, ENT consult, soft tissue neck XR or CT neck, IV access
Immediate assessment
Position pt upright (if tolerated)
check severity: stridor, voice changes, inability to lie supine, respiratory distress
Call for help early (anesthesia, ENT, surgery)
Keep pt calm; avoid agitation
Initial Interventions
Oxygen: Highflow oxygen (consider nasal high flow 1-60 L/min if avail)
Treat underlying cause:
Anaphylaxis: IM epinephrine 0.3-0.5 mg (1:1000)
Angioedema: Consider epinephrine, antihistamines, steroids
Infection: Antibiotics, steroids (if needed)
Foreign body: Heimlich maneuver or direct removal
Temporizing measures:
Heliox (80% helium/20% oxygen) if avail
Nasopharyngeal airway
Bagvalvemask ventilation (if needed)
Definitive Airway Management
Indications for intubation:
Inability to maintain oxygenation/ventilation
Progressive obstruction despite treatment
Stridor at rest, severe voice changes
Inability to handle secretions
Decreased level of consciousness
Extensive facial/neck burns or trauma
Intubation approach:
Preferred: Awake fiberoptic or video laryngoscopy (if difficult airway predicted)
Alternative: Rapid sequence intubation (if airway anatomy favorable)
Have rescue plan ready: LMA, cricothyroidotomy kit
Surgical Airway (if intubation fails)
**Imaging NOT delay airway management:** If pt is in distress, secure airway first
**Lateral neck XR:** Thumbprint sign (epiglottitis), prevertebral soft tissue widening (retropharyngeal abscess), steeple sign (subglottic stenosis)
**CT neck with contrast:** Gold standard for deep space infections (Ludwig, retropharyngeal, parapharyngeal abscess), hematoma, tumor. Only if pt is stable enough
**Flexible nasolaryngoscopy:** Direct visualization of supraglottic & glottic structures. Best diagnostic tool if avail & safe to do
**Cuffleak test:** Preextubation: deflate cuff, occlude ETT, check air leak around tube. No leak: ↑ risk of postextubation stridor
**CBC, BMP, lactate:** Infection workup, metabolic status
**BCxs:** If infectious etiology suspected: before abx if feasible
**ABG/VBG:** If respiratory distress: check ventilation & oxygenation
**Tryptase:** If anaphylaxis suspected: send within 12h of onset

pairs.value: Conscious: Abd thrusts (chest thrusts if obese/pregnant). Unconscious: CPR with airway checks. Direct laryngoscopy with Magill forceps for visible FB. If below cords: rigid bronchoscopy
IM epi first. If laryngeal edema progressing: early intubation (smaller ETT, video laryngoscopy). Surgical airway if CICO
Do NOT agitate. Double setup: OR with most experienced intubator + ENT for surgical airway backup. Awake fiberoptic preferred if avail. Smaller ETT (12 sizes down)
Awake fiberoptic intubation preferred (trismus limits DL). Have surgical airway ready. Do NOT paralyze: loss of muscle tone causes complete obstruction. ENT/OMFS for I&D
Awake intubation if cooperative. Risk of rupture & aspiration during intubation. CT neck first if stable. Surgical drainage by ENT
Neb racemic epi + dexamethasone. If refractory: reintubate (smaller ETT). Consider prophylactic steroids preextubation in high risk pts
Emergent bedside neck opening if airway threatened: cut sutures/staples, evacuate hematoma.thensecure airway. Do NOT wait for OR
Intubate early: edema worsens over 12-24h. Once swollen, intubation becomes extremely difficult. Large ETT (edema will narrow around it)
Awake fiberoptic intubation or tracheostomy under local. May need rigid bronchoscopy. Avoid paralysis: tumor may cause complete obstruction.

drugs.name: Racemic epinephrine (neb)
drugs.dose: 2.25% solution: 0.5mL in 3mL NS nebulized. Alt: Lepinephrine 5mL of 1mg/mL neb
drugs.contraindications: None absolute in airway emergency
drugs.notes: Mucosal vasoconstriction: ↓ airway edema. Effect in 10-30 min. May rebound: observe ≥2h after. Can repeat

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.dose: 10mg IV (adults). Can give 0.6 mg/kg IV/PO in pediatrics
drugs.contraindications: None absolute in airway emergency
drugs.notes: Give early: onset 4-6h. ↓ Airway edema for inflammatory/infectious/postextubation causes. May give preextubation prophylactically in high risk pts

drugs.name: Epinephrine (IM)
drugs.contraindications: None absolute in anaphylaxis
drugs.notes: Firstline for anaphylaxis related airway obstruction. Does NOT work for bradykininmed. angioedema (ACEI). See Angioedema topic

drugs.name: Heliox (70:30 or 80:20)
drugs.dose: inhalation via tightfitting NRB or vent
drugs.contraindications: High FiO2 requirement (>40% limits heliox effectiveness)
drugs.notes: Heliumoxygen mix: lower density: ↓ turbulent flow: ↓ WOB in partial obstruction. Temporizing bridge while definitive tx is arranged

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone
drugs.contraindications: Severe cephalosporin allergy
drugs.notes: Empiric abx for epiglottitis, deep space infections. Add vancomycin if MRSA concern. Alt: ampicillinsulbactam 3g IV q6h

drugs.name: Ampicillinsulbactam
drugs.contraindications: Penicillin allergy (use clindamycin 600mg IV q6h)
drugs.notes: Broadspectrum for Ludwig angina & deep space infections: covers oral flora incl anaerobes. Alt: penicillin G + metronidazole

Some air movement present. Stridor, voice changes, ↑ WOB. Canprogress to complete. Keep pt calm, do NOT agitate
No air movement. Unable to speak, cough, or breathe. Silent. Cyanosis. Immediate intervention required
Highpitched sound from turbulent airflow through narrowed airway. Inspiratory = supraglottic. Expiratory = subglottic. Biphasic = fixed obstruction.
Can't Intubate, Can't Oxygenate: indication for surgical cricothyrotomy. Final common pathway in airway emergency
Located between thyroid & cricoid cartilage. 1 fingerbreadth below laryngeal prominence. Site for emergency surgical airway

Anxiety; preference to sit/lean forward; inability to speak or voice change (muffled, hoarse); stridor (inspiratory = supraglottic, expiratory = subglottic, biphasic = tracheal/critical); choking, coughing, drooling; dysphagia; tachypnea, accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, tracheal tug

No stridor with worsening respiratory distress = near-total obstruction — the noise disappears when there is almost no air movement; this is a pre-arrest finding

sections.title: Investigations
items: Diagnosis is clinical — don't delay treatment for investigations if the airway is at risk
ABG: hypoxia, hypercapnia (late sign — normal PaCO₂ in patient with high WOB = patient is tiring)
FBC: ↑ WBC in infection
Coagulation screen: if hematoma or coagulopathy suspected
Blood cultures + oropharyngeal swabs if infection source
Imaging (only in stable patients with secured airway): neck X-ray AP & lateral, CXR, or CT neck/chest (reveals masses, foreign bodies, mediastinal abnormalities, epiglottis swelling)
Nasendoscopy by experienced ENT: can visualize level of obstruction — !!never attempt nasendoscopy in an unstable patient without a secured airway plan in place!!
Direct laryngoscopy: only if airway already secured or all preparations for immediate intubation/surgical airway are in place — can precipitate total obstruction

sections.title: Management
items: **Scenario 1 — Cardiac/respiratory arrest**: BLS → open airway with adjuncts + suction → remove obvious obstruction → start CPR → attempt immediate intubation → surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy) if intubation fails

**Scenario 2 — Peri-arrest (imminent arrest)**: call anesthesia + ENT STAT → immediate laryngoscopy/intubation attempt → prepare surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy) as primary backup if intubation fails

**Scenario 3 — ↓ Consciousness (intoxication, head injury, CVA)**: call anesthesia → assume C-spine injury if traumatic (manual in-line stabilization, NOT hard collar); airway always overrides C-spine concerns → OPA/NPA + BVM → RSI → cricothyroidotomy if intubation fails

**Scenario 4 — Swelling, infection, or physical obstruction (awake patient)**: call senior anesthesia + ENT → formulate airway plan (Plan A: ETT; Plan B: LMA; Plan C: surgical airway) → arrange equipment for awake fiberoptic or inhalational induction → transfer to OR if patient is stable
--Temporizing measures while arranging definitive airway: nebulized epinephrine 5 mg (1:1000) in 5 mL; humidified O₂ or Heliox (70:30 or 80:20); IV dexamethasone 8–16 mg
--Do NOT give sedation or anxiolytics to a partially obstructed, spontaneously breathing patient — they may completely obstruct with loss of tone
Early intubation is always better than waiting — partial obstruction → complete obstruction can progress in minutes
Cricothyroidotomy is indicated when: intubation fails AND ventilation fails; all other options exhausted; or as primary plan under local anesthesia for total obstruction with patent cric membrane

pairs.value: IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg (1:1000) immediately; IV antihistamines + corticosteroids; early airway if angioedema progressing — angioedema from anaphylaxis responds to epinephrine

Epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids are less effective than in allergic angioedema; specific treatments: C1-INH concentrate (Berinert/Cinryze), icatibant, tranexamic acid, or danazol for hereditary type; early intubation if airway involved
Remove dressings, cut sutures to decompress hematoma immediately; can relieve airway compression; still needs intubation — don't delay
Nebulized racemic epinephrine 2.25% or L-epinephrine 5 mg; IV dexamethasone 8 mg; apply CPAP/NIPPV; reintubate early if worsening; consider elective tracheostomy for prolonged cases

BVM with PEEP; apply jaw thrust; avoid excessive stimulation; if persistent: low-dose propofol 10–20 mg IV or succinylcholine 10–20 mg IV (laryngeal dose) — have intubation equipment ready immediately

Treat like laryngospasm (BVM, PEEP); IV neostigmine 2.5 mg + glycopyrrolate 0.5 mg if non-depolarizing block beginning to wear off; sugammadex 2–4 mg/kg IV for vecuronium/rocuronium (immediate full reversal)

If conscious: encourage coughing; back blows + abdominal thrusts (Heimlich); if unconscious/arrest: begin BLS, look in mouth before each ventilation attempt, remove visible foreign body; rigid bronchoscopy or direct laryngoscopy for retrieval

Do NOT use OPA/NPA (can burst abscess/provoke total obstruction); keep patient calm and upright; call anesthesia + ENT emergently; awake fiberoptic or inhalational induction preferred; IV antibiotics after airway secured

sections.title: Further Management
items: Transfer to ICU/critical care after airway is secured
Head of bed 30–45° to promote venous drainage and reduce edema
IV dexamethasone 8–16 mg to reduce ongoing airway edema
Lung-protective ventilation strategy if intubated (TV 6 mL/kg IBW, Pplat <30)
Sedation and ventilation may be required for days until cause resolves
Cuff-leak test + direct laryngoscopy before extubation to assess resolution of swelling
Consider elective tracheostomy if prolonged intubation expected or re-obstruction risk is high after extubation
Surgical/ENT/microbiology consult as needed for underlying cause

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Delaying intubation — partial obstruction can become total obstruction within minutes; early is always better
Giving sedation to a spontaneously breathing patient with partial obstruction — loss of muscle tone = complete obstruction
Nasendoscopy or direct laryngoscopy without a full surgical airway backup plan in place — can provoke total obstruction
OPA or NPA insertion in retropharyngeal abscess — can burst the abscess and soil the airway
Trusting that normal SpO₂ means the airway is safe — hypoxia is a late sign; a patient can tire and arrest with SpO₂ still in the 90s
Missing silent chest — absence of stridor with worsening distress = near-total obstruction, not improvement
Treating bradykinin-mediated angioedema (ACE-I, hereditary C1-INH) with antihistamines/steroids alone — these don't work; use specific agents
Cricothyroidotomy hesitancy when it is the only option — in a 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' scenario, a surgical airway is the only life-saving option

drugs.name: Epinephrine (nebulized)
drugs.dose: 5 mg (5 mL of 1:1000) neb; or racemic epinephrine 2.25% 0.5 mL in 3 mL NS
drugs.contraindications: No absolute contraindication when airway at risk
drugs.notes: Temporizing measure for post-extubation edema, croup, or mild-moderate allergic angioedema; onset 5–10 min; rebound swelling possible within 2–4h — monitor closely after

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.dose: 8–16 mg IV; repeat 8 mg q6–8h for ongoing edema
drugs.contraindications: Active infection (relative — use if airway at risk)
drugs.notes: Reduces airway edema from inflammation, post-extubation edema, croup, or angioedema; onset hours — NOT immediate; use early in anticipation

drugs.name: Heliox (70:30 or 80:20)
drugs.dose: Deliver by tight-fitting NRB at 15 L/min; titrate FiO₂ based on O₂ component
drugs.contraindications: Severe hypoxia requiring high FiO₂ (helium displaces O₂)
drugs.notes: Less dense than air — reduces turbulent flow through stenotic airway, ↓ WOB; temporizing bridge to definitive airway; most effective with >70% helium

drugs.name: Succinylcholine (low-dose, laryngospasm)
drugs.dose: 0.1–0.2 mg/kg IV (10–20 mg); full RSI dose if intubation planned
drugs.contraindications: Hyperkalemia, burn/crush/denervation injury >24h, known malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
drugs.notes: Low 'laryngospasm dose' breaks laryngospasm without full paralysis; have intubation immediately ready; onset 30–60 sec

drugs.name: Sugammadex
drugs.dose: 2 mg/kg IV (moderate block); 4 mg/kg IV (deep block); 16 mg/kg IV (immediate reversal of rocuronium RSI dose)
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity; does not reverse succinylcholine or benzylisoquinoliniums
drugs.notes: Reverses rocuronium or vecuronium; 16 mg/kg dose given immediately after 1.2 mg/kg rocuronium for 'can't intubate' rescue — fastest available reversal strategy

drugs.name: C1 Inhibitor Concentrate (Berinert)
drugs.contraindications: Not for allergic angioedema (epinephrine preferred)
drugs.notes: For hereditary angioedema (C1-INH deficiency) or ACE-I-induced angioedema; also consider icatibant 30 mg SC; do NOT rely on antihistamines/steroids for bradykinin-mediated angioedema

Primary spontaneous: tall, thin, young male, smoker. No underlying lung dz
Secondary spontaneous: COPD (most common), asthma, CF, PNA (necrotizing), PCP, TB, lung cancer, Marfan, LAM
On mechanical ventilation: barotrauma from high PEEP, high VT, air trapping (status asthmaticus)
Recent procedures: subclavian/IJ central line, thoracentesis, pacemaker, lung biopsy
Anticoagulation status (hemothorax risk)

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Sudden pleuritic chest pain + dyspnea + unilateral ↓ breath sounds; tension PTX = hemodynamic collapse + tracheal deviation + JVD — needle decompression before CXR if patient is crashing
Tension pneumo signs: ↓ BP, tachycardia, JVD, tracheal deviation away from affected side,Hypoxia (50% nonintubted; 90% intubated) hyperresonance to percussion, cyanosis, PEA arrest
Simple pneumo: ↓ breath sounds unilaterally, ± pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea. May be subtle
Hemothorax: ↓ breath sounds, dullness to percussion (vs hyperresonance in pneumo), signs of hemorrhagic shock if massive
Subcutaneous emphysema: crepitus on palpation (air tracking through soft tissue)
Chest wall: tenderness, instability, flail segment (multiple rib fractures)
In ventilated pt: sudden ↑ PIP, ↓ compliance, ↓ SpO2, ↓ BP, difficulty bagging: think tension pneumo

sections.title: Management

pairs.value: Immediate needle/finger decompression, then chest tube; 2nd ICS midclavicular or 5th ICS midaxillary; no imaging delay.

Stable + small: conservative mgmt, O2, analgesia, observe, repeat CXR; discharge if stable. Large/symptomatic: aspiration, pigtail, or chest tube. Small, stable PSP in a nonventilated pt may observed with O2 & serial CXR.
Low threshold for drainage; PPV or hemodynamic compromise = chest tube; traumatic tension = decompression first, then tube.

Smallbore or pigtail acceptable for pneumothorax; largebore tube for blood/clot; 4th-6th ICS anterior or midaxillary line. Typical sizing: 28-32 Fr for pneumo, 32-36 Fr for hemothorax. Connect to underwater seal/Pleurevac with 20 cmH2O suction & get postprocedure CXR.
VATS for persistent air leak, recurrence, bilateral disease, hemopneumothorax, or high risk occupation; not routine for first PSP.
>=300-500 mL or unstable: largebore chest tube; drain early, resuscitate, involve trauma/thoracic surgery.
>1500 mL initial or >200 mL/h x3h: decompress, restore blood, MTP, urgent VATS/thoracotomy evaluation; consider autotransfusion where available.
<300 mL + stable: conservative mgmt, repeat CXR up to 24h; avoid retained blood >300 mL.
VATS first line, ideally within 5 days; surgery for instability, retained hemothorax, persistent air leak, or diaphragmatic injury.
Warm saline irrigation may reduce reintervention; antibiotics for penetrating trauma, retained hemothorax drainage, or operative mgmt.
Do not delay decompression for imaging; chest tube output alone can mislead; fibrinolytics only if poor surgical candidate.
Visceral pleural line (pneumo), meniscus/opacification (effusion/hemothorax). Do NOT delay for tension pneumo: clinical dx
Most sensitive. Occult pneumo, sizing, bulla/bleb identification. Get if stable & dx uncertain
Fastest bedside dx. Absent lung sliding = pneumo. Lung point = specific finding. Free fluid in dependent thorax = hemothorax

If hemothorax or surgical intervention anticipated

Mandatory after chest tube placement or needle decompression
Monitor hourly.>1500mL initial or >200mL/h x3h = massive hemothorax: thoracotomy

sections.title: Chest Tube Insertion
items: Position: supine or semireclined, arm abducted overhead on affected side
Site: 4th-5th ICS, anterior axillary line (triangle of safety)
Prep, drape, local anesthesia (lidocaine down to pleura)
Make 2-3cm skin incision along rib (one interspace below target). Dissect bluntly with Kelly clamp over TOP of rib (avoid neurovascular bundle on inferior rib margin)
Puncture parietal pleura with clamp: expect rush of air (pneumo) or blood (hemothorax)
Finger sweep pleural space to confirm intrapleural position & clear adhesions
Direct chest tube (28-32 Fr pneumo, 32-36 Fr hemothorax) posteriorly & apically. Advance until all holes are within pleural space
Connect to underwater seal/Pleurevac, apply suction (20 cmH2O)
Secure with suture (0 silk), apply sterile dressing
CXR now: confirm placement, lung reexpansion, no residual pneumo/effusion
Document: tube size, position, initial output (volume & character), air leak presence

drugs.name: Lidocaine 1%
drugs.dose: 10-20mL local infiltration at chest tube insertion site
drugs.contraindications: Allergy
drugs.notes: Infiltrate skin, subcutaneous tissue, periosteum of rib, intercostal muscles, parietal pleura

drugs.name: Procedural sedation
drugs.dose: Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg IV or fentanyl 1-2 mcg/kg + midazolam 1-2mg IV
drugs.contraindications: Hemodynamic instability (use cautiously)
drugs.notes: For awake chest tube placement if time permits. Do NOT delay for sedation in emergent cases

drugs.name: Ketorolac
drugs.contraindications: Renal failure, active bleeding, coagulopathy
drugs.notes: Rib fracture pain. Adequate analgesia prevents splinting: atelectasis: PNA

drugs.name: TXA (tranexamic acid)
drugs.dose: 1g IV over 10 min (within 3h of injury if traumatic)
drugs.contraindications: Active intravascular clotting
drugs.notes: For massive hemothorax as part of MTP. Consider intrapleural TXA in select cases

pairs.value: Air in pleural space without mediastinal shift. May be small (<2cm at apex) or large
Oneway valve: air enters but can't escape. Progressive pressure: mediastinal shift: ↓ venous return: obstructive shock: PEA arrest. Clinical dx: treat before imaging
"Sucking chest wound": defect in chest wall communicating with pleural space. Cover with 3sided occlusive dressing,thenchest tube
Blood in pleural space. Massive = >1500mL initial or >200mL/h ongoing. Causes: trauma, iatrogenic, aortic rupture, tumor, coagulopathy
Air + blood: may need 2 chest tubes (apical for air, basilar for blood)
Seen on CT but not CXR. If pt being ventilated: still needs chest tube (risk of converting to tension)

pairs.value: ↑ airway RESISTANCE (peak reflects resistance). Causes: secretions/mucus plug, kinked or bitten ETT, bronchospasm, water in circuit. Fix: suction, bite block, bronchodilators, clear tubing. Check plateau with inspiratory hold.

↓ COMPLIANCE (plateau reflects alveolar/lung-chest wall). Causes: pneumothorax, mainstem intubation, worsening edema/ARDS, auto-PEEP, abdominal distension/↑intra-abd pressure, chest wall rigidity. Risk of barotrauma — investigate urgently.

pairs.key: Low pressure / low exhaled Vt / low MV
pairs.value: Leak or disconnect: circuit disconnection, ETT cuff leak (audible, ↓return volume), dislodged/near-extubation, bronchopleural fistula / chest tube leak. Check connections and cuff pressure.
No spontaneous effort — oversedation, neurologic decline, or trigger not sensed. Confirm mode delivers mandatory breaths; lighten sedation if inappropriate.

Pain, agitation, anxiety, metabolic acidosis (compensatory), dyssynchrony, or auto-triggering (leak, cardiac oscillation, condensate). Treat cause — don't just sedate. Rule out acidosis before ↑ sedation.
Starting mode; mandatory rate + guaranteed Vt delivered at/above set RR. Vent does all the work. Adjust ventilation (CO₂): ↑ RR or ↑ Vt. Adjust oxygenation: ↑ FiO₂ or ↑ PEEP.
Patient-triggered, flow-cycled; vent adds set pressure above PEEP per effort. Used for weaning — better tolerated, exercises respiratory muscles. No backup breath if patient doesn't trigger.
Target SpO₂ 92–96%. Wean FiO₂ to <0.6 first (O₂ toxicity risk at >0.6 prolonged). PEEP recruits collapsed alveoli (↓ shunt); too much PEEP → overdistension + ↓ CO.
Target PaCO₂ / pH. ↑ RR or ↑ Vt → ↑ minute ventilation → ↓ PaCO₂. Lung-protective targets: Vt 6 mL/kg IBW, Pplat <30, !!driving pressure (Pplat − PEEP) <15!!.
Incomplete exhalation → intrinsic PEEP → ↑ peak pressure, ineffective triggering, hypotension (obstructive physiology). Quantify with expiratory hold. Treat: ↓ RR, ↑ expiratory time, bronchodilators.
Treat pain/anxiety and optimize mode/settings BEFORE deepening sedation or paralyzing. Watch the flow/pressure waveforms — the pattern names the problem.

Effort that doesn't trigger a breath. Cause: auto-PEEP (COPD/asthma), weak effort, trigger too insensitive. Fix: ↓ auto-PEEP (↓RR, ↑ expiratory time, bronchodilators), ↑ trigger sensitivity, treat obstruction.
Vent delivers breaths without patient effort. Cause: circuit leak, condensate/water, cardiac oscillations, trigger too sensitive. Fix: ↓ sensitivity, clear condensate, fix leak.
Patient demand > set flow (scooped-out pressure waveform), air hunger. Fix: ↑ inspiratory flow rate, switch to pressure-control/PRVC (variable flow), ↑ Vt if appropriate, treat pain/anxiety.

Two stacked breaths → high delivered volume, barotrauma risk. Cause: inspiratory time too SHORT relative to neural demand. Fix: ↑ Ti / Vt (as lung-protective limits allow), sedation; consider volume-targeted adjustment.
Ti mismatched to patient. Premature (Ti too short): ↑ Ti or ↓ cycle-off %. Delayed (Ti too long, seen in COPD): ↓ Ti or ↑ expiratory cycle-off % (e.g., 40–50%).
If severe (esp. ARDS) despite optimized settings + adequate analgo-sedation → consider short course of neuromuscular blockade (cisatracurium). Paralysis requires deep sedation + analgesia first.

sections.title: Sedation & Analgesia Principles
items: Analgesia-first (analgosedation): treat pain before adding sedatives — reduces total sedative need
Target light sedation (RASS 0 to -2) unless a specific indication for deep sedation (severe ARDS, refractory dyssynchrony, status epilepticus, ↑ICP, paralysis)
Assess pain (CPOT/BPS) and delirium (CAM-ICU) on every shift; use daily spontaneous awakening (SAT) + breathing trials (SBT)
Avoid benzodiazepines for routine ICU sedation — more delirium and longer vent days (PADIS guideline); prefer propofol or dexmedetomidine
Match the agent to the physiology: shock → ketamine or opioid-first; agitation/weaning → dexmedetomidine; deep sedation/↑ICP → propofol
Sedation weaning: taper precedex 25% q6h, benzos 25% q24h, opioids 25% q24h — minimize cumulative burden; delirium risk rises with higher total sedation load

drugs.name: Fentanyl
drugs.contraindications: Chest-wall rigidity with rapid high-dose push; additive hypotension/resp depression with sedatives
drugs.notes: **MOA:** mu-opioid agonist. **Physiologic effects:** analgesia + mild sedation, blunts respiratory drive/RR, hemodynamically neutral (mild). Analgesia-first agent. No active metabolites — safe in renal failure. Lipophilic: accumulates with prolonged infusion.

drugs.name: Propofol
drugs.contraindications: Egg/soy allergy; hypotension/shock; additive resp depression & hypotension
drugs.notes: **MOA:** GABA-A agonist. **Physiologic effects:** rapid on/off sedation, anticonvulsant, ↓ICP; dose-dependent hypotension (vasodilation + ↓contractility) and resp depression. Watch PRIS (metabolic acidosis, rhabdo, ↑TG, arrhythmia) at high dose/prolonged use. Lipid load 1.1 kcal/mL.

drugs.name: Dexmedetomidine
drugs.contraindications: Advanced heart block, bradycardia, hypotension; additive with other AV-nodal/negative chronotropes
drugs.notes: **MOA:** central alpha-2 agonist. **Physiologic effects:** cooperative sedation with minimal respiratory depression, analgesia-sparing, less delirium; bradycardia + hypotension (transient HTN if loaded). Best for light sedation, weaning/extubation. Not for deep sedation or paralysis cover.

drugs.name: Ketamine
drugs.contraindications: Caution: severe uncontrolled HTN, tachyarrhythmia; emergence reactions
drugs.notes: **MOA:** NMDA antagonist. **Physiologic effects:** dissociative sedation + potent analgesia, bronchodilation, preserved airway reflexes & respiratory drive, hemodynamically stable (endogenous catecholamine release). Useful in shock, bronchospasm, opioid-tolerant patients.

drugs.name: Midazolam
drugs.contraindications: Delirium risk; accumulates in renal/hepatic impairment (active metabolite); CYP3A4 interactions
drugs.notes: **MOA:** benzodiazepine (GABA-A). **Physiologic effects:** sedation, amnesia, anxiolysis, anticonvulsant; respiratory depression, hypotension. Reserve for status epilepticus, alcohol withdrawal, deep sedation. More delirium & vent days vs propofol/dex (avoid routine use).

drugs.name: Cisatracurium
drugs.dose: Bolus 0.15–0.2 mg/kg; infusion 1–3 mcg/kg/min, titrate to TOF
drugs.contraindications: MUST have deep sedation + analgesia first (paralysis ≠ sedation); potentiated by aminoglycosides & Mg
drugs.notes: **MOA:** nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker. **Physiologic effects:** skeletal muscle paralysis; Hofmann elimination (organ-independent — good in renal/hepatic failure). Short early course for severe ARDS dyssynchrony. Risks: awareness if under-sedated, ICU-acquired weakness. Monitor train-of-four.

pairs.value: 5/5 PSV (PS 5 cmH₂O, PEEP 5) × 30–120 min. Fail criteria: SaO₂ <90%, PaCO₂ ↑ >10 mmHg, RR >35, HR >140 or <50, SBP <90 or >180, agitation/diaphoresis/↑ WOB.
P:F >150, PEEP ≤5, FiO₂ ≤0.4, pH >7.25, HD stable, intact cough, manageable secretions. !!~15% reintubation within 48h is expected!! — don't let fear of failure delay extubation of ready patients.

If cuff leak absent or high risk (female, prolonged intubation, prior stridor, large ETT): methylprednisolone 60 mg IV q6h × 4 doses (or single dose); plan extubation 4–6h after last dose.

Standard: day 14. Early (day 7–10) if prolonged ventilation clearly expected (high SCI, severe TBI, poor neuro trajectory). No proven mortality benefit of early vs. late; may reduce sedation requirement.

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: **Key question**: recent exposure to an oxidizing agent? Ask specifically — patients don't always volunteer these
**Topical anesthetics**: benzocaine (especially cetacaine spray, OTC gels), lidocaine (large doses), prilocaine (EMLA)
**Medications**: dapsone (most common drug cause), primaquine, rasburicase, phenazopyridine (Pyridium — turns urine orange), chloroquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin
**Nitrates/nitrites**: amyl nitrite ('poppers'), sodium nitrite, industrial nitrate exposures, contaminated well water (infants — 'blue baby syndrome'), sodium nitroprusside (prolonged high-dose)
**Other**: hydroxylamine, aniline dyes, nitric oxide (inhaled — ICU setting), metoclopramide (rare), rasburicase (G6PD patients)
G6PD deficiency: ask family history; if G6PD-deficient — methylene blue will fail and may worsen hemolysis → exchange transfusion
Congenital MetHb: cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency — lifelong mild cyanosis, not acute emergency; well-compensated at baseline
Infants <4 months: fetal Hb more easily oxidized; at-risk for nitrate-contaminated water

pairs.value: SpO₂ fixed around 85% despite escalating O₂ + chocolate-brown blood on ABG — pulse-ox is unreliable in MetHb; get co-oximetry and ask about oxidizing agent exposure (dapsone, benzocaine, nitrites)
Falsely reads ~85% regardless of actual MetHb level — !!the pulse-ox is not reliable here!!; does not change with O₂ escalation
Chocolate-brown blood is pathognomonic — visible in IV tubing, on filter paper; doesn't turn red with O₂ exposure (unlike deoxyhemoglobin)
Central cyanosis disproportionate to perceived distress (mild MetHb); progresses with rising MetHb%
MetHb >20%: headache, anxiety, dizziness; >30%: fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia; >50%: AMS, seizure, coma; >70%: potentially fatal
Clear — hypoxemia is a hemoglobin problem, not a lung problem; WOB usually mild unless concurrent lung pathology
Tachycardia (compensatory); ↓BP if severe (MetHb >50%); dysrhythmia rare unless coexistent
Cyanosis present even with SpO₂ 'normal' on co-oximetry (hallmark); gray-brown tinge in severe cases
Oxidizing agents convert Fe²⁺ (ferrous, O₂-carrying) → Fe³⁺ (ferric, non-functional); methemoglobin also shifts O₂-Hgb curve left (↑ affinity → poor O₂ delivery to tissues)
Most common drug cause; used for PCP prophylaxis, dermatitis herpetiformis, leprosy; hydroxylamine metabolite is the oxidant; onset hours–days after starting
Topical anesthetic sprays (cetacaine): rapid onset during/after procedures (upper endoscopy, bronchoscopy, intubation); can cause severe MetHb quickly
Amyl/butyl nitrite ('poppers'), sodium nitrite (food preservative overdose, cyanide antidote kit), industrial exposure, well water (infants)
OTC urinary analgesic (Pyridium); turns urine/sclera orange — a visual clue; MetHb with overdose or renal failure (drug accumulation)

Artifact (nail polish — acetone it off; poor pleth; venous pulsations); sulfhemoglobinemia (sulfonamides, metronidazole; no treatment; resolves over weeks); CO poisoning (SpO₂ falsely normal, not 85%)

sections.title: Management
items: **Stop the offending agent** — always step 1; dapsone has a long half-life so MetHb can recur; may need repeat methylene blue doses over 24–72 hrs
**100% O₂ by NRB**: maximizes dissolved PaO₂ and O₂ delivery from residual functional Hb while antidote is prepared; does not reverse MetHb
**Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV** over 5 min: first-line antidote; works within 30–60 min; response confirms diagnosis
- Check MetHb at 60–90 min post-dose; if MetHb >10% or symptoms persist, repeat 1 mg/kg
- Max total dose ~7 mg/kg (paradoxically causes MetHb at high doses)

**G6PD deficiency**: methylene blue won't work (requires NADPH, absent in G6PD deficiency) and can cause hemolysis → consult hematology; options: exchange transfusion, hyperbaric O₂, ascorbic acid 1–2 g IV (weak/slow effect)

**Dapsone-induced MetHb**: often recurs due to long half-life → admit for serial MetHb levels; N-acetylcysteine 600 mg PO q8h may reduce hydroxylamine levels; cimetidine inhibits CYP2C9 (reduces dapsone toxicity, limited evidence)
**Exchange transfusion**: last resort for refractory MetHb or G6PD patients; removes oxidized Hb and replaces with functional RBCs
**Hyperbaric O₂**: if available and MetHb refractory; increases dissolved O₂ to maintain tissue oxygenation while MetHb clears
~~**Orders**: ABG with co-oximetry (not standard pulse-ox), CBC (hemolysis?), G6PD level, BMP, LFTs~~
Co-oximetry ABG: gold standard — reports OxyHb, DeoxyHb, MetHb, COHb as % fractions
CBC: hemolysis (Heinz bodies on smear, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin) especially with dapsone or G6PD deficiency
G6PD level: critical before giving methylene blue; send before treatment if time allows (won't hold up treatment in extremis)
Standard pulse oximeter: unreliable — reads 85% regardless of actual MetHb; co-oximeter required

pairs.value: Normal (baseline)
Cyanosis, may be asymptomatic; chocolate-brown blood
Headache, dizziness, fatigue, exertional dyspnea, anxiety, tachycardia
Marked dyspnea, syncope, chest pain, AMS, weakness
Seizures, coma, severe acidosis, dysrhythmias
Potentially fatal; !!treat before this level!! — threshold for treatment is usually >20–25% or symptomatic at any level

sections.title: Common Mistakes & One-Liner
items: Escalating O₂ (NC→NRB→HFNC) when SpO₂ is 'stuck at 85%' without checking co-oximetry
Trusting the pulse-ox — in MetHb, the standard SpO₂ is meaningless; only co-oximetry reveals the truth
Ordering a standard ABG without specifying co-oximetry — the PaO₂ will look reassuringly normal
Forgetting to ask about benzocaine sprays (used by proceduralists/anesthesia), 'poppers,' or dapsone — exposure is often missed without direct questioning
Giving methylene blue to a G6PD-deficient patient — will fail and precipitate hemolytic crisis
Not repeating methylene blue doses in dapsone toxicity — dapsone's long half-life means MetHb recurs hours after the first dose
One-liner: !!SpO₂ ~85% that doesn't respond to O₂ + chocolate-brown blood = methemoglobinemia until proven otherwise — get co-oximetry and give methylene blue!!

drugs.name: Methylene Blue
drugs.dose: 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min; repeat 1 mg/kg in 30–60 min if inadequate response; max ~7 mg/kg total
drugs.contraindications: G6PD deficiency (ineffective + hemolysis); high doses (>7 mg/kg) paradoxically cause MetHb; caution with serotonergic drugs (serotonin syndrome risk)
drugs.notes: First-line antidote; MOA: NADPH reduces methylene blue → leukomethylene blue → reduces Fe³⁺ back to Fe²⁺. Onset 30–60 min. Turns urine/skin blue transiently. Will interfere with subsequent pulse-ox readings.

drugs.name: Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C)
drugs.contraindications: Less effective than methylene blue; not first-line
drugs.notes: Second-line: nonenzymatic reducer of MetHb; slower onset; use when methylene blue is contraindicated (G6PD deficiency) or unavailable. Doses up to 3 g/day used in mild-to-moderate cases.

drugs.name: N-Acetylcysteine (NAC)
drugs.dose: 600 mg PO q8h (adjunct in dapsone toxicity)
drugs.contraindications: Not a primary antidote
drugs.notes: Adjunct in dapsone-induced MetHb: replenishes glutathione, reduces hydroxylamine generation. Not a substitute for methylene blue.

items: CHECK NOW
